I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but if I deemed it advisable to touch upon the question of the tobacco illustration station situated at L'Assomption, it was because the hon. minister had just explained he was asking for much larger appropriations for salaries on account of the increase in the number of experimental farm officials all over the country.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: (Translation.) That may be germane to the question, but barely so.

The minister
stated in answer to my question that no experimental farms had been closed. I pointed out that the experimental farm at L'Assomption had been closed. I was sure there were some employees there receiving salaries from the Government. We are now considering the question of salaries of employees on experimental farms as well as other employees of the Government, and it is perfectly in order to discuss the salaries of these men.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are not considering the salaries of employees on experimental farms throughout the country.
Does the item not refer to salaries of all employees of the Department of Agriculture?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item which we are now considering refers to salaries paid to all employees of the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa.
Civil Government is what we are discussing now.

I bow to your ruling, Sir, but may I suggest this for your reflection? I think in the English House of Commons it is not an uncommon thing to move a reduction of salaries and on that basis to discuss the whole department. I grant, however, it would be much more convenient if your ruling could be carried out.
Perhaps the discussion was brought about through a reference of the minister to an increase in the work of experimental farms. I am not questioning the ruling at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It Was precisely on that feature that the discussion came up, and it was also for that reason that the Chairman did not interrupt the hon. member (Mr. Seguin). He merely drew the attention of the committee to the matter after the hon. member had concluded his remarks.

May I suggest to the
minister that he go over the increases item by item and explain to the committee the increases in the work or other necessities justifying the increase in the number of employees.
What item?
I would suggest beginning with the first item of that class, head clerks, increase three to four, principal clerks, increase four to six, and so on, each one in sequence.

That was due to a change in the classification. This man is a very efficient officer, one of the best we have in the department, one who is thoroughly versed in his work and one whom I have found, in my brief time in the office as minister, a very valuable man.

I see by last
year's Estimate that there were only three head clerks, now there are four. I admit this clerk may be very intelligent, but he cannot double himself.
This man has been promoted,'and a position beneath him filled, making four instead of three.
The work which was done last year by three man cannot be done now by three?
No, if we wish to obtain the efficiency we desire.

Has the minister before
him the names of these four head clerks with rather good-sized salaries?

No, but I shall be glad
to furnish them later.
In what branch is this new head clerk?
In the deputy minister's office.

I notice the salary of the deputy minister is fixed at $5,500. I understood that the salaries of other deputy ministers had been fixed at $6,000. Why is this deputy minister receiving $500 less than other deputies?
He has a house allowance, which accounts for the difference.
Does that house belong to the Government?

Yes, it is situated on the
Experimental Farm. The present deputy minister was Director of Experimental Farms, and resides there in the house he had before, and is always available for giving his valuable advice in the work of the farm.

Would it not be better to fix the salary at $6,000 and charge him $500 rent?
TMr. Tolmie.]

The deputy minister
seems to be quite satisfied with the present arrangement, and we have found no objection so far.

I would be disposed to be very generous to the Department of Agriculture, because I do not think we have been spending enough money on that department as compared with other departments of the Government. I find by the Auditor General's Report that there has been an apparent extravagance in travelling expenses. The travelling expenses shown at page A-14 of the Auditor General'^ Report, referring to the headquarters' staff I presume, amount to the large sum of $55,276.70. I think the minister ought to give some explanation of that. In looking over the names, I find that in one case, at all events, the amount spent in travelling expenses exceeded the amount of the man's salary, and in other cases the travelling expenses are quite large. Why is it necessary to spend such a large sum as $55,276.70 in travelling expenses?

We have recognized that travelling expenses have become a very important item, particularly on account of the increased railway fares, the great increase in hotel bills these men have to pay, the increased rates on dining cars, and for hiring cars to take them from place to place about the country, and so forth. Several of our divisional officers have necessarily to do a lot of travelling in order to carry on their work. In the Health of Animals branch, for instance, the men have to travel from place to place. In Alberta and Saskatchewan, in connection with clearing up the mange, we had a large number of men travelling over an area of 2,600 miles. We have fruit inspectors moving from one part of the country to the other, and livestock promoters out in the field working up the live stock business, encouraging breeders to co-operate in their methods of marketing their stock to the very best advantage, and so forth. Then there are the Experimental Farm superintendents and the inspectors of Illustration Stations. All these men require a large amount for travelling expenses. It has become a very large item, and we have given a great deal of consideration to it, but until there is a general fall in prices, I do not see how we can reduce travelling expenses very soon.

Instead of having men travelling from Ottawa to different parts

of the country, would it not be possible to have men located at different points throughout the country, who at the same time would be in constant touch with the authorities at Ottawa? Why could not that be done to save travelling expenses? I would think that men on the spot would understand the conditions better.

We have men on the spot now, but the "spots" are very big. For instance, a fruit inspector in British Columbia has to mave about among the other inspectors who are permanently located at different points. The chief inspector goes about exercising general supervision over their work. The same is true of the Health of Animals Branch. A man might be located at Ottawa, and there might be an outbreak of hog cholera 200 miles away. There is nobody closer to that point than himself, and so he has to travel that 200 miles and back again, and pay his hotel bill while he is engaged there. We are attempting to curtail travelling expenses as much as possible, so far as is consistent with rendering efficient service to the livestock and other agricultural interests.

I do not think this item of
$55,276.70 covers the travelling expenses of the inspectors who are out in the field, because provision is made in different parts of the Estimates for that. I think this large item refers to the head office staff here in Ottawa.

We have a number of
heads of different branches located in the city of Ottawa, such as the Director of the Experimental Farms, the Veterinary Director General, the Assistant Veterinary General, the Livestock Commissioner, the Chief of the Fruit Markets Branch, and many others. We find that to keep these men up to date and thoroughly abreast of the work being carried on throughout the country, and so that the field inspectors may benefit by their better knowledge of the whole situation, it is necessary for the branch heads to visit the different parts of the country at least once during the year. We find that has a very stimulating effect on the work being carried on. The chief inspectors in the different provinces are very glad to see the man from headquarters. I speak with a good deal of feeling on that point, because I was Chief Inspector of the Health of Animals Branch and representative of the Livestock Commissioner in British Columbia for many jears. One or two years might elapse without my ever seeing anybody from 'headquarters, and I know how a person is inclined to drift from the ordinary lines under those circumstances. We find it very beneficial to have a headquarters man going around throughout the country to keep everything working uniformly.

I notice that on page 89
provision is made for a Chief, Poultry Division ; Chief, Sheep and Goats Division; Chief, Cattle Division; Chief, Horse Division; but no provision is made for Chief, Swine Division. Not because I am personally interested, but for the good of the country, I would like to know what has become of the swine.

The swine are included
[DOT]with the sheep and goats.
When the minister comes to separate the sheep from the goats, where will he find the swine?

The minister has told
us that the deputy minister is occupying the house he occupied as Assistant Director of the Experimental Farm. Might I ask what housing provision has been made for the present Assistant Director?

The deputy minister
occupies the house he occupied as Director of the Experimental Farms, not Assistant Director. The present Director occupies the house he occupied as Assistant Director.

There is no
assistant director?
There is an assistant director, Dr. Shutt, of the Experimental Farm system. He resides at the Central Farm in Ottawa.
Does the gentleman who took the place of the present deputy minister reside on the farm at present?
Yes.
Would the officials of the department be entitled to lower transportation rates over Government roads?
We used to get a rate over different lines, at one time as low as a cent a mile. Later on it was increased somewhat. That concession has been discontinued entirely now.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to the present expensive cost of food on dining cars. I think this matter should be brought forcibly to the attention of the Minister of Railways. Members of the House, and

citizens generally who travel to any extent, will quite appreciate what the minister says in regard to the cost of meals on dining cars throughout the country. It might be possible for the Minister of Agriculture to take this matter up with the Minister of Railways. Something should be done, at any rate, because the dining car rates to-day are more exorbitant than they should be in view of the amount of food supplied the patrons of the different railways for the prices charged. The people feel strongly on this question, and I am glad that the minister has referred to it. It is one that could be dealt with very satisfactorily between the Minister of 'Agriculture and the Minister of Railways, and if something could be done to reduce the rates on dining cars, it would be highly appreciated.
What disposition is made of the products of the Experimental Farms?
They are sold, and the money is turned in to the Receiver General.

Before we leave the question raised by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig), with regard to travelling expenses of officials, now that Canada owns such an immense mileage, are instructions given to Government officials as to what roads they should travel over when going from one part of the country to another where both roads run?
Yes, in our department they are instructed to use, as far as possible, Government roads, Government express, and Government telegraph service.
Are those instructions carried out?

Wherever practicable,
but in some parts of the country it is impossible to avoid the use of the other roads.
When they want to get from one place to another in time, what are they instructed to do?

I certainly do not rise to encourage any extravagance at this time;
I know that the country cannot afford to spend too much. But I see that a great deal is being expended in agricultural salaries one way and another, and I desire again to call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to the fact that year in and year out, on the floor of the House, I have been asking his careful attention to the study of the agricultural condition in the

northern part of the county of Wright,-
I do not mean its extreme north, because it extends almost to the North Pole. The county is very large, and it afforded me much pleasure to be present last fall at an exhibition held in Maniwaki, which is about 98 miles from Ottawa. The exhibition was a great credit to the place. It brought numerous exhibitors together and demonstrated just what could be produced in the way of agricultural products as far north as anything could grow. They have put up a building there, in the construction of which I understand the Government has aided. I marvelled at the building they were able to erect for the sum of money which it actually cost. In another portion of the county, in the town of Aylwin, there is always a splendid exhibition, but, of course, it is the most populous part of the county. At that exhibition they show stock, poultry, and field products, and it has been of immense benefit it the people living in the lower end of the county. I have found that agricultural lectures serve a great purpose, and I have particularly requested an experimental station, or rather two. There could be a station at one end of the county, and another up north. It seems a lot to ask for, but it would result in incalculable good. I do not want to increase expenditures unnecessarily, for I believe in economy; but owing to the varied conditions in that county, to its altitude in certain parts, at least two experimental stations are necessary, one in the northern, and the other in the lower part of the county. I speak now for the county of Wright; not for that part of the county which, up to 1917, was included in Wright, and which is known to-day as the county of Hull.

I shall be glad to look into the matter carefully. Perhaps illustration stations would be more suitable than an experimental farm, because they could be located at a small expense, and would be useful in demonstrating to the farmers of the immediate vicinity under what conditions the best results in agriculture could be obtained.

I do not want to repeat a question asked on a previous item, but will the minister please indicate in what branches there has been an increase in the number of employees? At page 90, for instance, we have head clerks, of whom there are four now as compared with three last year. The minister has .

given a reason for that increase. In the next item there are six instead of four, then eight instead of seven, twenty-one instead of sixteen, and so forth. Will the minister indicate in what branches there have been increases in the number of employees, and for what reasons?

In the first one there is one increase, a senior clerkship. That was in the Health of Animals Branch. The Health of Animals Branch has extended a good deal during the last year on account of the development of the Accredited Herd System, and the outbreaks of hog cholera this year have also been much more numerous, making it necessary to carry on a great deal more record work than in the past. The next increase of clerks has been in the Experimental Farm system, as well as in the Health of Animals Branch system. With reference to the latter branch the same answer that I gave before to the hon. member applies.
Do I understand that it is at the Experimental Farm that the increase has occurred?
In the Health of Animals Branch, and also in connection with the Experimental Farm. The two together would account for the increase. Does the hon. member require any further information?
I want the whole list.

The next item with respect to junior clerks is relative to the Health of Animals Branch. In the item dealing with senior accountant clerks the changes have been in the accountants branch of the Department of Agriculture. The item relating to senior clerk stenographer applies to the Health of Animals and Livestock Branches.
I notice there is an increase of seventeen stenographers.

In the case of the clerk stenographers this applies to the Health of Animals Branch, the Livestock Branch, and the Seed Branch. The junior clerk stenographers that are referred to are in the Seed Branch, the Livestock Branch, and the Experimental Farm. The clerk typists referred to are in the Seed Branch, the Livestock Branch, and the Health of Animals Branch. The item referring to office appliance operators has to do with the Publications Branch.

Would the minister be kind enough to inform me who is in charge of the cattle which are distributed throughout the country by the Department of Agriculture. I would like the minister to state the name of the official, his salary, and where his headquarters are located?
The Live Stock Branch is under the supervision of Mr. H. S. Ar-kell, Livestock Commissioner, whose salary is $4,200 a year.
Were any cattle distributed by the department last year? If so, in what localities did the distribution occur?

I will give the hon.
gentleman all the details. A large number of cattle have been distributed throughout the whole of Canada, because the system is a very popular one. I shall be very glad to state the places to which they have been sent but at present we are discussing an altogether different item.
Upon whose recommendation is the distribution made?

The applications are
sent into the Livestock Branch by various clubs under certain conditions, and the applications are carefully looked into by the representatives of our branch. Mr. Hamer represents Mr. Arkell in this matter, and if the application made is in strict conformity with the regulation and the conditions are found to be satisfactory, a distribution is made. If such is not the case, the application is refused.
When the animals are thus distributed are they given away by the department, or must they be returned after the expiration of a certain length of time?
They are simply loaned.
Can the minister tell me if the cattle which were distributed in my constituency in 1917 have been returned to the department?

To what part of the
country does the hon. member allude?

I am very much surprised that the minister should have to inquire the name of my constituency. Since the minister has taken charge of his department he has shown great efficiency, and has also displayed great devotion to the interests of the farming class in Canada. I would advise my hon. friend to be kind enough, after the recess, to come into my

constituency and then he will learn that it is one of the best farming constituencies in the province of Quebec. In that connection, and referring to the question which I just put to the minister, if my hon. friend does come to the county of Dorchester he will find there lots of cattle that belongs to his department. Those cattle were placed in my constituency by a very generous government during the election a few years ago.
A bad recommendation for your county.

It is a very bad recommendation for the Government, not for my county. The minister has inquired as to the name of my constituency. Now that I have told him, and also informed him where the constituency is situated, I hope he will show towards that county the same interest he has displayed towards the rest of Canada, and especially towards his own province of British Columbia.

If time permits I will be very pleased indeed to accept the kind invitation of the hon. member for Dorchester to visit his constituency next year and look into its agricultural prospects. When I make that visit I sincerely hope I shall find the hon. member at home.

I am always there.
Mr, TOLMIE: Since last session I have made every effort to visit as many parts of the Dominion as I possibly could. I have been in Quebec on several occasions, but I have not seen half enough of that province. I hope at the first opportunity to extend my visits to those parts of the country that I failed to reach on previous occasions. As regards the distribution of these bulls and other livestock, the distributions are made absolutely free of any political considerations. I have worked in this particular line myself in British Columbia, and in every instance we considered whether the group of men or club had fully complied with the regulations, and if we found they had not they got no animals, if they had met all the regulations, we gave them the best animals we could get for the money. We have 266 bulls at the present time in the province' of Quebec, distributed there by the Livestock Branch. I could not give details of their distribution at the moment, but I will be very pleased to furnish this information if my hon. friend wishes it.	,
Have horses been distributed by the department?
Under the old system we used to distribute horses under the same conditions as we distribute cattle, sheep, and swine, but that system has been changed.
When was it changed?
I think about three years ago.	.
Were any complaints received by the department from the district of lake St. John as to the distribution of horses there by the department?
Not that I know of. It was before my time.
Might I inquire what item is before the committee? I am sorry I was not in the House when these Estimates were taken up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The item before the committee is No. 14 on pag 8 of the Estimates, but the explanation of that item is to be found on pages 89, 90 and 91.
Then I assume that the matter that has been under discussion is not pertinent to the item before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The discussion on
the distribution of livestock would be more in order under item 49, where a special amount is provided for livestock.

I presume that
this item applies to the inspectors of livestock throughout the country who are on the permanent staff. Are these inspectors, who I believe are graduates of the veterinary school, appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

The inspectors in the
Livestock branch and the Health of Animals branch are appointed by the Civil Service Commission.

This item of
$541,955 is very large, and in connection with it I want to say a word or two about some of the inspectors of livestock. It is quite evident that a considerable change comes over some people when they get permanently in the service-they become very autocratic and domineering. I have in my constituency a man who considers that he has been very badly used not only by the inspectors but also by the Department of Agriculture itself. This man raises hogs. An inspector from the department examined the hogs and said they were diseased and that he would come around in a day or

two and destroy the whole herd. My constituent denied that there was any disease in his herd, that on the contrary he had not lost a hog for two years, and that if any cholera existed among them surely there would be some evidence of it through the hogs dying, because the disease works very rapidly as a rule. A number of the animals were fit for market and the owner asked to have the privilege of dressing the carcases and disposing of them if the animals were going to be destroyed, The inspector gave him the privilege of dressing all he could in one day. Thirty-three of the best finished hogs were dressed and hung up for the inspector's examination. He examined the intestines and did not find any disease, and the carcases were disposed of for food. But the inspector destroyed every other animal-there were 245 in the herd-and refused to give the owner any compensation. Now, we have been passing legislation in regard to compensation, but I do not think there is anything in the statutes covering such a case as I have represented. It is true that certain authority is given to the department to make regulations, and I am informed that it is under those regulations that this action was taken. I am merely calling the attention of the minister to the very peculiar manner in which some of the inspectors in his department acted in this particular instance. All the aggrieved party asks is that a commission be appointed to investigate the matter, and he will abide by their decision. But the department will not consider the suggestion. I even had the temerity to write a letter to the Veterinary Director General, and I am told that one of these understrappers in the department made the remark, that Mr. Sutherland had better attend to his own business and they would attend to theirs. Now, if that is correct, and they are the class of men that we are voting salaries to to-day, I think we should know something more about them before we pass this item of over half a million dollars, particularly in view of the statement made by the head of the Civil Service Commission yesterday, and published in the press this morning, in which he practically dictates to the members of this House what they shall do, and imputes motives to them that no employee should be permitted to impute and remain in the service of the Government.
Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the minister
should have an opportunity of replying to the question.

In reply to what the
hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) has said, it must be borne in mind that hog cholera is not a disease which shows itself very clearly in all cases. Where the disease is very acute the animal dies within a few hours and the symptoms are clearly defined; but should the animal be suffering from chronic cholera there would be no external symtoms and to the eye of the layman the hog would be apparently healthy. So far as our Health of Animals branch is concerned, I want to say that it is the most efficient, not merely on this continent, but in the whole world. Our men are all graduates of recognized veterinary colleges and in addition have passed a stiff Civil Service examination as well as an examination under the Health of Animals branch, with a view to ensuring their qualification for the important work they have to undertake. Having myself been one of these men, I know the ups and downs of the business very well. In many cases where a man's animals have been destroyed he sees that there is a loss of money and he is very much hurt. He cannot, perhaps, trace the source of infection; he cannot understand why the animals should be sick, and in some cases it is very difficult to please him. But I am quite sure that the reports of these inspectors could be depended upon if they made a diagnosis and found hog cholera, because my deputy minister has mentioned some of their names and I find that among them are one or two of the best we have in the Health of Animals service. , I shall be very glad, as long as I have the honour to preside over this department, to receive complaints from anybody regarding any of our officials who are not courteous or who do not carry out their duties in the proper way. If any such cases are brought to my attention, I promise to make very careful investigation of the circumstances. The member for South Oxford has already mentioned this particular case to me. I have sent for a report, but it has not yet come to hand; I expect it at an early day.

I would like to say
just a word in regard to this matter of appointment of officials. If I could not make any better appointments than some that are made by the Civil Service Commission I would consider myself absolutely incompetent to give an expression of opinion upon

anything. In regard to these inspectors, I do not know how many there are in connection with the Health of Animals branch, but it would appear to me that the staff cannot be a very large one, or else they take things very leisurely. There was an outbreak of glanders in the northern part of my county last year, and on the 14th of October inspectors came out to that district, quarantined three or four farms, shot half a dozen animals or more, and gave strict instructions as to the carrying out of certain regulations, telling the farmers that they might not under any circumstances allow a horse to come on their farms until the Government lifted the quarantine. They also informed the farmers that they would be back in thirty days to make a further inspection and that they would then inform the farmers whether or not they could be freed from the quarantine regulations. The 14th of November came around, but no inspector appeared; the 14th of December passed, and still no inspector. These farmers wrote me in regard to the matter. I called up the department by telephone, and apparently it was only then that they remembered that there was a place out in the north of Frontenac which had been visited by their inspectors and in which some animals had been shot and a quarantine established. Indeed, it was only after they had been reminded of the matter several times over the telephone that they got busy and did anything; it was not until well on in January that the quarantine was lifted. What I complain of, and what these farmers complain of, is this: if there are not enough of these inspectors to attend to the business at the proper time, then more should be appointed. When these inspectors said they would return in thirty days, they should have returned in thirty days. As it was, the farmers could not prepare their ground for the next year's crop; they could not even get out their potatoes or anything of that kind, and on the whole they were left in a very bad position as regards their crop for this year. I think that was absolutely unnecessary; it would not have occurred had these inspectors cared, as I submit they should have cared, about the way in which they performed their duties. The trouble with a lot of people in the Civil Service to-day-and we have repeated instances of it-there is no use shutting our eyes to the fact-is that they feel that they are absolutely independent of this Parliament and they do not give a hang what we say or what we think. They hold their 
meetings; they say through the head of their commission and others the most impertinent things. They impute to members of this House motives that they have no right to impute to them, as did, according to the papers, the chairman of the commission the other day. What right has Hon. Dr. Roche, even though he was a member of this House and a member of the Government at one time-what right has he to say that because I choose to take a view in regard to this matter which differs from his view, I am actuated by a motive to hold the whip hand over people in my county? I resent any such attitude or any such words on the part of the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission. If the gentleman had not occupied a seat in this House and a seat in the Government at one time I do not think he would have felt that he could go quite as far as he has gone in expressing opinions derogatory to members of this House. With any person not so high up in the scale as the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission we would have no hesitation at all in characterizing such words as absolute impertinence, and even though he does occupy the position of Chairman of the Civil Service Commission I want to say here and now that I so regard the words which he made use of in speaking in the city of Ottawa, if he is correctly reported in the papers of yesterday and to-day.
Something is wrong in regard to this Health of Animals Branch. These men should have returned when they said they would. It seems to me that they were indifferent; that is the only way that I can look at it-they were indifferent as to what the effect would be upon these farmers in my county. I want to say, Mr. Chairman, through you to the Minister of Agriculture, as I will to the minister of any other department of this or any government while I hold a seat in this House, that no department or government in Canada will show indifference to any of the people of the county I represent and get away with it.

Perhaps a word of explanation, Mr. Chairman, will throw a little light on the subject. I am very sorry indeed if the farmers of any part of Frontenac have been inconvenienced in any way owing to the fact that inspectors could not reach their premises and release them from quarantine just when they promised to. But there are extenuating circum-

stances, I think. For instance, in undertaking the accredited herd work throughout the whole of Canada we were astounded how popular the work was with the farmers; a great many more went into it than we had anticipated. In addition, the big work was on in Alberta in connection with the elimination of mange, and we had an extra number of hog cholera outbreaks last year, so that there was an extreme shortage of qualified veterinary inspectors. To give you an idea, Mr. Chairman, as to what changes have taken place in the veterinary profession as a result of the fall in the price of horses, let me say that there graduated from the Ontario Veterinary College last year, the largest college of the kind in Canada, only twenty-five men or thereabouts, whereas in 1891 I remember quite distinctly that 225 men graduated from that institution. The field of operations for the veterinary is not so large as it used [DOT] to be. Consequently, many of our young men, with the high prices prevailing and the good opportunities offering in other lines, have not taken up veterinary work, and we have a good deal of difficulty in securing qualified veterinary surgeons to carry on the work of the health of animals branch. In this connection we are not entirely alone because, while we are, I think, one or two hundred herds behind in the way of applications, in the United States, with their accredited herd system, they are many thousands of herds behind in their applications. Their work thus shows that there is a shortage there also. I am sorry to hear that these men were inconvenienced, and I will use my best efforts to see that that sort of thing does not occur again.

Last year I succeeded in obtaining for certain farmers in my constituency certain books called "Farmers' Account Books." Some were in English, and I had to apply to the Commission of Conservation to have them translated into French. I succeeded in having that done, but I am told that now the Commission of Conservation is going to be abolished. Will the minister tell us to whom we shall now have to apply to obtain these books, which are very valuable to farmers especially in view of the fact that they have to make income tax returns like anybody else.

I cannot give the hon. member exact information now, but that is a matter that will be taken up in the
event of the Commission of Conservation being eliminated.
Will those books be in French?

We will do what is right. At six o'clock the committee took recess.
