speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at six o'clock we were considering the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture. We had reached and quite fully discussed item No. 14 on page 8 of the Estimates, the details of which are to be found on pages 89, 90, and 91 of the Estimates for the current year. Shall item No. 14 carry?
With reference to the footnote on page 9, would the minister inform the committee what part of the salaries are carried under the War Appropriation and Demobilization votes?
These contingencies are for clerical and other assistance, printing and stationery, sundries and travelling expenses. The details will be found on page 91.
My hon. friend wants to know what part of these salaries comes under War Appropriations and Demobilization.
None of it.
Then what do the asterisk and footnote mean?
There is still some correspondence in connection with the Food Board that is being carried on by Mr. Stephens, the principal clerk to the deputy minister. He received no extra salary for that work.

I do not think the minister yet understands my hon. friend's question. Opposite the item of salaries for the Department of Agriculture there is an asterisk, which is explained by the footnote on page 9, "These votes include salaries and contingencies carried under the War Appropriations and Demobilization votes." If that is correct a certain part of the item for salaries comes under the War Appropriations and Demobilization votes, and we want to know just how much.
The only work that would come under that is the answering of correspondence in connection with the Food Board, for which no extra salary is given to the principal clerk who does that work.
Then why is this reference made to the footnote?
I presume a portion of his salary is attributed to that. He spends from one to three hours a week in connection with the work of the Food Board.
How much would it be in dollars and cents?
Probably from $30 to $50 a year, roughly speaking.
That comes out of this vote?
Yes.
Is that extra salary?
No.
How much of the whole, appropriation for civil government is to be expended in connection with the Dominion experimental farms?
I could not give that as a total, but I could give it item by item, which would take some time.

Can the minister say what proportion will be expended in connection with experimental farms in the province of Ontario? My reason for trying to get this information is that I made quite an effort last session to get it, and I was told that the per capita expenditure for the province of Ontario was greater than that of any other province in Canada. My observations would lead me to the conclusion that the province of Ontario was doing this work itself and paying for it, as well as contributing to the expenses of the other provinces. In answer to a question I placed on the Order Paper last year as to what was the amount paid in salaries at the Central Experimental Farm under the head of Civil Government for the year

1918-19, the total given was $93,295.95. There is a very large expenditure on this farm that has evidently been charged against the province of Ontario, although it is well known that the work of the farm is not confined to Ontario, but is carried on for the benefit of the whole Dominion. The farm is the centre of the whole system in operation throughout the Dominion, and I for one must refuse to have the total expenditure for this central farm charged up against the province of Ontario, and to be told that the per capita expenditure is greater for Ontario than for any other province. I have for years strenuously objected to the manner in which Ontario was being discriminated against in the matter of experimental farms.
How many experimental farms have you in Ontario?

There is a small tobacco farm at Harrow, about 487 miles from the central farm at Ottawa. There is another farm at Kapuskasing, 542 miles to the northwest of Ottawa, in the bush in northern Ontario. So far as I know, those are all that are being carried on in the province, with the exception of. the central farm, the work of which is, in my opinion, more beneficial to some of the other provinces than it is to Ontario. We were told this afternoon that even a part of the salary of the deputy minister is charged up against the expenses of this farm. The salary of the deputy minister, I understand, is more than that of others in view of certain perquisites which he has in con-* nection with the farm. Before this item passes, I think we ought to know exactly whether the expenditure for the experimental farms, particularly under the head of Civil Government, is anything like equal throughout the Dominion:	My own view
is that it is not. Ontario has been continually discriminated against in this matter, although it is doing the work and payng for it besides contributing to the expenses of the other provinces.

Does the hon. member think that the experiments conducted by the farm here would benefit the other provinces, particularly in the West, where climatic conditions are different, to the same extent as they would the province of Ontario? I think that these expenditures should be charged against this province. The experiments conducted at this farm would be of no particular benefit to us, because our climatic conditions are different.

The headquarters
of the whole system of farms are situated here; the officers are here all the time, and the work is beneficial to Western as well as Eastern Canada. The work on the farm here serves the adjoining province of Quebec much more than it does the province of Ontario.
I was not speaking of Quebec but of the western provinces.

I was speaking of both Western Canada and Quebec. I was informing the hon. gentleman that this was the headquarters for the whole system, operating in Western Canada as well as in other parts of the Dominion, and he says that this ought to be charged up against Ontario because the work is of no benefit to Western Canada.
The experiments conducted here are of no use to Western Canada. At all events, it is obvious that they are more beneficial to Ontario than to a province where conditions are different.
The item under discussion is Civil Government expenditures; it is not a matter of experimental farms at all.

About three-quarters of it would come under the head of Civil Government. The whole staff of the experimental farms comes under the head of Civil Government. I regret that we cannot give the total. I could give it item by item, but that would take a good deal of time. In connection with the Central Farm, we have appropriated $396,858.50; in connection with Kapuskasing, in northern Ontario, $35,405; and in connection with the Harrow tobacco farm, $6,231. The experiments conducted at the Central Farm are beneficial to many other provinces. A good deal of general work is done, such as experiments in connection with new plants-as, for instance, varieties of wheat, such as Marquis and Ruby wheat, different kinds of oats, and one or two varieties of barley-and while this is beneficial to Ontario, it is also useful to the whole of Canada. Take, for instance, the sunflower experiments this year. We have produced from twenty-seven to thirty-two tons of sunflower to the acre, and put it into the silo at $2.70 per ton. That is something of the greatest benefit to the people of the whole country; it is useful to farmers all over the country who are
interested in these special lines of experiment. It must be remembered, however, that the mere fact that the farm is located here is of immense benefit to the province of Ontario, because it is easily accessible to the farmers of that province who can take the train, or in summer, come down in their motor cars and see the work being done, thus benefiting directly.
What are the qualifications and responsibilities of those designated head clerks?

These are men who
assume a certain amount of responsible work in their various departments. They carry on important correspondence and also investigation, to some extent, and they usually have three or four clerks under them. In a limited way they are supervisors.	*

I asked vvhat their
qualifications were.

They have to pass a
Civil Service examination, and a good many of them are university men.

I asked this question because I see that the salaries paid run up to $3,200. On page 89 the salary of the superintendent of the farm is, however, only $2,340. Does the minister think that these salaries bear any proper relation to the qualifications and the responsibilities of the respective officers?
What particular officer does the hon. gentleman refer to?

I was saying that the salary of the superintendent of the farm is only $2,340, whereas the salaries of the head clerks go as high as $3,200. What relation is there between those salaries and the responsibilities of the men engaged in the different classes mentioned?

The superintendent of
the farm is, of course, immediately under the director. The clerk the hon. member speaks of is a man who, as I say, assumes a certain amount of the responsibilities of the office. It is very difficult to state exactly whether one is more valuable than the other. If that farm superintendent were left to his own resources I should imagine his responsibilities would be very much greater; but I think we all now realize pretty well that these matters are fixed by the Civil Service Commission. There are, perhaps, a good many things done of which we do not approve but we cannot help it.

We have had considerable discussion about the Civil Service Commission, and the only way in which we can determine the value of the work that it is doing is by making inquiries of this kind. Personally I cannot see any relation between the qualifications required from, and the responsibilities incurred by, a man who has charge of an experimental farm and a clerk in an office. It seems to me that the salaries paid in this case are not relatively proportionate to the responsibilities incurred.
I may say that the salary of the superintendent of the farm will finally go up to $3,000. He also has a free house, which is heated for him, and that is an added advantage.
I notice there is a gentleman who separates the sheep from the goats. He is paid $3,000, whilst the superintendent of the farm only receives $2,300. Why is there that much difference?

These salaries are all
fixed by the Civil Service Commission. The man who "separates the sheep from the goats," to quote my hon. friend's words, does work throughout the Dominion. He has to be familiar with local conditions in various parts of the country, and a great deal more general knowledge is demanded of him than of another man who may be an expert in a particular department.

Has he been successful in
separating the sheep from the goats?

I have not heard of any
quarrels among them yet.

I would like to know the reason for the increase of $8,000 in the Entomological branch? My reason for asking the question is that for years in the West grain growers have been suffering from certain insect pests. One is the saw-fly which attacks our wheat; in fact the ravages of this pest have 'reached such a stage that some growers have about decided to forego the growing of Marquis wheat in my area. The ravages of the sawfly are largely responsible for this determination among the farmers. Then the grasshopper pest has worked havoc for the past three years in a large area out there. I was wondering whether this $8,000 additional was to be applied to the solution of the problem of combatting evils such as those I have alluded to. I believe that in certain parts of my constituency no less a sum than $10,000,000 has been lost in the last

three years owing to the depredations of these insects; and we have been very much interested in learning whether the Dominion and provincial governments would not endeavour to provide some remedy that would successfully combat the attacks of insect pests. I would like to have an expression of opinion on the subject from the minister.

The crusade against
grasshoppers in Western Canada is carried on under the provisions of the Destructive Insect Pests Act, and the vote for that purpose will be found in the Estimates. I may say that we have been in the past few years co-operating with the provincial departments of agriculture in the carrying out of measures for the eradication of these pests, and I think that last year very satisfactory work was done. We have a number of experts who devote their whole time to that work out in the West. We have one in particular who accompanies a moving demonstration train throughout the western country giving lectures, and atfording other information, in connection with the measures for dealing with these pests. Last summer, with the co-operation of our men the provincial governments were able to substitute sawdust, and other things, for bran in connection with the poisoning of grasshoppers. They also conducted experiments with poison gas and found that putting poison in bran and other materials was far more satisfactory than the use of gas promised to be. We ate still continuing that work. I would like to extend the scope of the work of the department a good deal because I think there are a good many opportunities to do so, but of course we cannot carry out all our wishes having in view the financial situation in Canada. We therefore have to work with the brakes on, so to speak, in connection with this matter.

I notice, Mr. Chairman,
a considerable increase in the number of the employees under the item we are considering. Under the vote for Civil Government in connection with the Department of Agriculture, 318 employees were last year provided for. This year the Minister is seeking to make provision for 359, an increase of 41. Now I quite recognize the very great importance of the Department of Agriculture to the welfare of the Dominion; but at the same time consideration should be given to the financial position of the country and the fact recognized that it is time to exercise economy. We should therefore keep our expenditures, if possible, within the limits of what they were last year. I

was just wondering if it would not be possible for my good friend who presides over the Department of Agriculture to get along with the same number of employees that he had a year ago, and thus reduce the expenditure under this particular heading by anywhere from fifty to sixty thousand dollars.

I fully realize the financial condition of the country, and on any occasion when I find myself inclined to be a little neglectful of the fact in my enthusiasm for further expansion, I am promptly reminded of it by my colleague the Minister of Finance. With respect to the particular items to which the hon. member has referred, I may say that I explained them all in detail shortly before six o'clock. If my hon. friend reads to-morrow's Hansard he will there find all the details of our work as it is carried on throughout the country. We have been as economical as possible, but we feel that these increases are absolutely necessary if we are going to maintain the progress of agriculture in Canada.

I would like to
say a word or two before we get away from the subject of the experimental farms. Some hon. gentleman opposite drew the minister's attention, away from this particular matter, but I would like to institute a comparison between the two old Provinces of Ontario and Quebec where the conditions are very similar. At one time the Central Experimental farm served both these provinces, and there was no other Government experimental farm in existence, At the present time, however, I notice that in the province of Quebec there are five central farms and fourteen sub-stations. Four of these farms are very much closer to the Central Farm than are the two farms located in the province of Ontario. I have noticed the expenditure for labour on these farms and I presume that the votes for a good many of these men come under the head of civil government, for the men are permanent and are employed from year to year. I also notice that for the two farms in Ontario the expenditure was $17,521, whereas the expenditure for the same purpose in the province of Quebec was $65,869. This does not include the $93,000 paid out in connection with the administration of the Central Farm at Ottawa some of which I presume will be charged up against the province of Ontario. There is a large item in the Estimates for travelling expenses incurred by officers employed on this farm. I am not finding fault with the number of 595
the men, or the work they are doing but I have contended in the past-and I still contend-that Ontario is being very unfairly dealt with in this regard. We contribute about one-half of the revenue of this country, and we are either paying for or doing ourselves the work that the other provinces are having done for them by the Dominion. If the Government is going to continue in that course we should, I think, consider whether it would not be better to hand this work over to the different provinces and let them conduct their own affairs. Then we should have an equitable distribution in connection with this matter.

I may explain that none of these farms were located in the province of Quebec during my term of office, and the moneys to which the hon. gentleman refers as moneys paid out for the carrying on of the various farms do not come under the civil government vote and consequently not under the item which we are discussing at the present time.

I would like to ask the
minister if the department is taking steps -to rebuild the experimental flax mill which was destroyed by fire some time ago. So far as I can see there is no item in the Estimates providing for a continuance of that experimental work. I would like to know what the "attitude of the department is towards this industry.

We are having plans
prepared for a new flax mill to replace the mill that was destroyed. We have a certain amount of money in these Estimates which might be used towards re-building, and if it is decided to go ahead with the new mill we may have to get more money in the Supplementary Estimates to complete the work. I fully realize the importance of the flax industry and its possibilities, and I can assure the hon. member that I shall be very glad to render every asistance possible to its development.
Do I understand that the item under discussion does not cover the branch experimental farms at Kapuskasing, Harrow, Cap Rouge, Lennox-ville, Ste. Anne, and Farnham?
No.

While on the question of salaries, I think it has been recognized for years that officials in the Department of Agriculture are very much underpaid in comparison with officials in other departments. I am not going into the ques-

tion to-night, but I want to make one comparison. I notice that in some of the other departments a filing clerk receives a higher salary than professors in the different branches of the Department of Agriculture, such as assistant chemists, field husbandry men, and other technical men who have to spend years to qualify for their positions. I think there must be something radically wrong when a filing clerk is paid $100 more a year than the men I have described, and I would draw the minister's attention to the situation. I shall be willing to give him my support in any efforts he may make to place the salaries of these technical men on as attractive a basis as that obtaining in the other departments of the Government service. Perhaps the minister would like to voice his opinion on that point?

I think good men are
always worthy of their hire, and undoubtedly we have in the Department of Agriculture many men who are rendering very valuable service to this country-service which could never be put in dollars and cents. Dr. Saunders, who created Marquis wheat, made a very valuable contribution to the country at a time when an improvement in our wheat was very badly needed, and I am sorry that there is no way of recognizing his ability. I think that, generally speaking, the hon. gentleman is correct and that the merit of our technical men in the Department of Agriculture has not been recognized as fully as it has been in other departments of the Government. So far as I am concerned, I shall always be glad to do all I can to the end that these men may be paid as liberally as possible. We must make their positions attractive if we expect to retain good men. By underpaying them we are simply making the department a training school for the benefit of other governments; we find our best men are taken by the provincial governments and by the gov-eminent of the United States after we have trained them for three or four years.
Is every man employed at the experimental farms classified under the Civil Service Commission?
They are all classified except the labourers.
Is it the intention of the Department of Agriculture to expend any money during 1921 in experimenting on the treatment of flax fibre in the West.
It is the intention of the department to expend money on the experimental farms in the Prairie Provinces in connection with the development of the flax industry.
What are the average hours that men employed on the experimental farms are expected to work?

The average is about
nine hours in winter and ten in summer.

I am informed that
men employed on the experimental farms are sometimes obliged to work from twelve to fourteen hours per day without extra remuneration. I would like to know the policy of the Government in respect to these men.

Men like herdsmen and teamsters and others engaged in various lines of work where it is necessary for them to give attention to animals after their regular working hours are paid salaries, and they work on an average about eleven hours a day, but those are exceptions.

I think the minister
ought to be in a position to give this committee his definite views so far as the employees of the experimental farms are concerned in regard to how much they are paid for a ten-hour day, and how much they are entitled to if they work extra hours.

Day labourers work by the day and in Eastern Canada are paid about thirty to thirty-five cents an hour. If they work overtime they are paid at the same rate. In Western Canada they are paid from forty to forty-one cents an hour.

What is the policy of the Government in regard to these men, and how much are they paid when they work extra hours? I do not refer particularly to those engaged on the experimental farms in the province of Quebec, I am referring to those engaged on all the Government farms.

The rates as I have
stated them; they are not the same all over the country. If the men work an extra hour they are paid at the same rate.

I notice that in this
item a special sum is allotted to the library. Where is that library, what books are in it, and to whom are the books distributed?

The library is located in the West Block. It contains a large number of books dealing with agriculture. Books and publications are also kept there which are received in connection with the International Bureau of Agriculture, with headquarters in Rome, to the meetings of which we send a delegate every year. _We secure from that source very valuable information concerning crop production all over the world, the production of animals, and so on, and we are able to keep in close touch with market conditions and, in general, prospects for the future in agriculture. Improved methods in agriculture are also noted and those that we think suitable to our needs and conditions are tried out on our experimental farms.
I am well satisfied with the answer given by the minister. Are these books published in both languages ?

Some of them are.
Some, too, are published in more than two languages.
Are the books distributed throughout the country, and if so, to whom?

They are for the use of
the Agriculture Department. Of course, any reliable person can communicate with the department and take out one of these books for a time and subsequently return it.

I notice a strange
anomaly on page 90: "1 translator, $1,500; 1 junior translator, $1,550." Apparently it is best to be a junior if you are in the translating business.

That is fixed by the
Civil Service Commission. It can be explained by length of service in the department.

To try to palm this
off on the Civil Service Commission does not seem to be satisfactory. " Junior translator " connotes, to my mind, the idea that he is junior in the service to the translator, yet he gets $50 more. There must be some explanation of this, or some mistake has been made which should be corrected.

There are a great many
anomalies in the Civil Service re-classification. Under the old classification this junior translator was entitled to run up to $1,560. According to the ruling of the
commission, employees could not be paid less than they were receiving before. This translator has come in under the new classification.
What is the name of the translator and what is the name of the junior translator?

I regret I cannot give
the names just now, but I shall be glad to get them for the hon. gentleman.
How long have they been in the service and what are the reasons given by the Civil Service Commission for the salaries assigned to each?

The junior translator
has been in the service about six years, and the translator about two years. I cannot personally account for any action of the Civil Service Commission.

Is the minister positive
that the Civil Service Commission is accountable for the fixing of this salary?
Yes, as far as my information goes.	[DOT]

But we want to know whether or not the minister is prepared to state definitely that the Civil Service Commission is responsible for fixing the salary of this translator at $1,500 and of the junior translator at $1,550.

The Act is responsible
for the $1,550, and the Civil Service Commission is responsible for the other one.

I note that there is
provision for two junior zoologists at $1,295. I do not see any senior zoologist in the list. Why should there be two juniors and no senior?
There are no senior zoologists, and these two employees do not work in the same office. Both are women.

Will the minister inform me whether the men employed at the experimental farms are entitled to a holiday of fifteen days or so each year without reduction of salary, even if they are absent one or more working days throughout the year?

Those who work by the
hour lose their time if they remain off. Those who work on salary are entitled to the usual holiday period. If a man misses a day through sickness or something of that kind, it is not deducted from his holiday.

Do I understand then,
that if a man employed at the experimental farms is absent, say, ten days, and later, at different times, absent another five days, he will still get his fifteen days' holiday without suffering any reduction of salary?
In all those cases he must get permission from the Civil Service Commission before he is permitted to take those days.
Not at all. The minister is not serious there.

I do not know whether we should blame the minister for the further anomalies I purpose setting forth before the committee, or whether the Civil Service Commission is to blame but I would draw this to the attention of the minister, as it seems to constitute a grave injustice. A senior file clerk gets $1,525; one file clerk gets $1,600, or more than the senior; a junior file clerk gets $1,250, and junior file clerks are paid more than a great number of stenographers. I should imagine that the work of a filing clerk was purely mechanical, requiring only carefulness and industry, while to be a good typist one has to have a very substantial degree of education. Perhaps the minister is not to blame for this, but certainly it does not reflect great credit on whoever is responsible for drawing up these grades in the service.
Mr. TOLMIE The same explanation that I gave a short time ago under the same conditions apply to that.

That is that the Civil Service Commission is responsible, but that is really no explanation to the committee for these very startling anomalies. The higher grades of service are being paid on a lower scale of remuneration than the lower grades. That is not fair.

I should not like the minister to go on record as saying that employees on experimental farms are entitled to a holiday whenever the Civil Service Commission declares them to be entitled to one. I do not think the minister meant what he said a minute ago, and I should like him to give an answer again so that the committee will know exactly his position in the matter.

What I said is that they should get the authority of the Civil Service Commission before they could get a holiday. Those working by the hour are
not entitled to holidays with pay; they lose their pay if they take a holiday. Those on salary are entitled to the regulation holidays given to any other members of the Civil Service."

That is not the point I am aiming at. I should like the minister to state whether, if a man happens to take only five days at one time and then takes one day after another, he is entitled to fifteen days altogether without having his salary reduced.

As I understand the matter from the Civil Service Commission, it is not necessary for him to ask for the whole fifteen days if he wants five days, he can get them. If he is sick, he can get sick leave. The hon. member will find the provision in the regulations of the Civil Service Commission.

The minister, in giving or attempting to give explanations regarding the items of the Estimate we have before us, has exposed the weakness of the Civil Service Commission. He blames, and, I think, rightly so, all these anomalies that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMas-ter) speaks of, on the Civil Service Commission but in spite of the time spent by Arthur Young and Company, Griffenhagen and Company and the Civil Service Commission, there is still in the department of the minister, one poor unfortunate who has failed to be classified at all. Surely the minister will be able to tell us something about this person, what he does and what his salary is.
What item is the hon. gentleman referring to?
The last item on page 91 a civil servant not classified at all, with a salary of $1,600. What does he do?
I can get that information for the hon. gentleman in a few minutes.

With a view to pointing out to the minister that I am not talking simply for the purpose of embarrassing him, because I do not believe I could, I will give him a concrete case which is reported to me and which is a justification for my interfering at this particular point of the discussion on the Estimates. I am told that at some experimental farms, employees are working ten hours and sometimes twelve or more hours a day, and they deserve a good deal of credit for the

time they spend on these farms in the interest of the people at large. When the time comes to take a holiday and they ask permission from the superintendent of their farm, he will say to them: "You may have this day, but it will be deducted from your salary." Therefore, these people complain that they have no opportunity to have a holiday outside of the ordinary holidays of fifteen days in the year. While some of them may take their fifteen days at one time; others would rather take ten days and then keep five or six days during the year for other purposes, taking a holiday whenever they want it. If it happens that they do not take their fifteen days at one time, but keep a few days 9 p.m. for their own pleasure or purpose afterwards, when they take such a day, a day's pay is deducted from their salary. Whatever there is in the complaint, all I can say is that I have received it, and these people say that a strong injustice is being done to them by their salaries being reduced for a day's holiday although they spend so many hours working for the country. That is why I am asking the minister to state whether, if a man is entitled to fifteen days' holiday in the year, if he takes these fifteen days at one time or a day now and then, he is entitled to full pay and not to have his salary reduced because he takes a day or two now and then.

As I pointed out before, there is no objection to these men obtaining their holidays from time to time as may suit their convenience, but on every occasion, they must receive authority for doing so. If they use up their fifteen days in that way, their pay is not reduced.

That is just the point I wanted the minister to come to. There is, for instance, employed on an experimental farm at Charlottetown, a man who has a brother dying, for instance, in Quebec, and he has to leave at once. According to the view that the department is taking now, this man has to write to Ottawa in order to receive authority for one or two days' holiday. That is what happens, that has happened, and the minister should see that a situation like that is not tolerated any longer.

That is not exactly the "case. In an emergency of that kind, he has no trouble. He does not even have as much trouble as other people have under similar circumstances. He gets permission
from the superintendent and is allowed to go at once.
In the various classifications of stenographers, clerks and so on, are men and women doing the same class of work?
Yes.
Is any distinction made as regards salaries?
No distinction for similar positions.

Referring to translators,
I notice that the senior translator of the department secured this year an increase of $120. The translator is not classified as either senior or junior, but is simply put down as translator. He gets an increase of $60, while the junior translator gets an increase of $100. I should like to ask the minister, who fixes the amounts of these various increases, and what is the reason for making these distinctions between people who are apparently doing the same class of work. Why should the junior translator get a bigger increase than the translator?

The junior translator is
under the old classification and his salary is practically fixed by the Act. It could not be reduced to a lesser amount than he was receiving, and it goes on increasing at the old rate. The increases under the new classification, under which the others come, are fixed by the Civil Service Commission.

Am I to understand the minister to mean that the Civil Service Commission has the right to fix the wages that shall be received by the civil servants in the employ of the Government, without the head of the department having anything to say about the matter?
The salaries and the increases are fixed by the classification.

Does the minister refer
to the classification that was made by those American experts imported into Canada, or to some other classification?
The classification brought into force about a year ago.
By whom?
By the Civil Service Commission.

Last week the Minister of Trade and Commerce explained during a debate in this House that experts brought

into the country by the Government, and who were absolute strangers to the Civil Service had made certain changes in the classification of the civil servants. Am I to understand that the changes which appear in the item I refer to were made by the experts or by the Civil Service Commission itself?

I understand that these
salaries were fixed at the time the classification was made, but what part the American experts played in the classification I could not say off-hand.
What I want to know is who made the classification? The Civil Service Commission, the minister, or the outside experts?

It was certainly not the
minister, but the Civil Service Commission. Whether they had the assistance of these imported experts or not, I could not say.
The minister states he is not responsible for the classification of these employees?
The minister had nothing to do with the fixing of these salaries.

But before the classification was made was not the minister consulted by the Civil Service Commission or by the experts, because, after all, the people who can give proper information in regard to the employees of a department are the head, the deputy head, and the branch heads? Were they consulted, and if so, did they make reports written or verbal?
The classifiers had a staff of experts of their own, and also consulted the deputy head before the classification was approved.

Am I to understand that the deputy head of the Department of Agriculture is responsible for the classification of these particular employees. If so, I would like the minister, who is the head of the deputy head, to tell us the reasons for these varying increases.

The evidence of the
deputy minister was taken by the commission, who came to their own decision.

I should like to know
from the minister, now that his deputy is here and can give him the required information, why the junior translator is getting a bigger increase than the translator himself?

Although the evidence of the deputy minister was taken, the final 
decision was in the hands of the Civil Service Commission. Therefore, I do not hold the deputy minister responsible for these increases that appear here. As I have explained before, there is the old classification and the new. This particular class of junior translator begins at a salary of $1,200 under the old system, with annual increases of about $50 a year up to about $1,600. Under the new classification the minimum salary of translator is fixed at $1,440 with annual increases of $60 up to the maximum.
May I ask if the superintendents of the various experimental farms in this country are competent men?

They are, so far as I
know.
Then if they are, I should like to know why, when a man on one of these farms wants a holiday, he has to apply to Ottawa instead of to the superintendent of his particular farm?
In case of an emergency, a holiday is given by the superintendent of the farm, and authority afterwards obtained from the Civil Service Commission.
That just brings me back again to the same question.

I notice that these farm labourers receive a bonus of $420 in addition to their regular salary. About a year ago we obtained the information that the expenditure under the head of civil government for the experimental farm at Ottawa was $93,295.95, and that the wages paid to the farm labourers amounted to $163,831.87. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Parent) need worry himself so much about the holidays of these men on this little farm out here. They are having a pretty fair time considering the number employed and the wages paid them. Over a quarter of a million dollars is being paid in salaries out here on this farm on the outskirts of the city, and I think the amount is altogether too great considering the results from the farm. I believe that the gooner a radical reform is instituted in connection with the experimental farm system in this country, the better it will be for Canada. I think that an example should be set those who are engaged in agriculture in this country, instead of having a great show place for the whole country when they come to Ottawa The work carried on at the farm is largely lost to the average farmer, and a quarter of

a million dollars, under present conditions, is altogether too much to spend in connection with a farm of this kind. I do not think, furthermore, that these expenditures should be charged up against the province of Ontario, which, we are told, is being benefited thereby. I do not see what ground there is for telling us that we ought to be satisfied, when we have to do the experimental work ourselves on our own farms and pay for it.

I see there is
an increase in the number of messengers from eleven to thirteen. What are the duties of these messengers?
They carry fresh eggs.

I shall answer first the statement of the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland). It is true that a great deal of money is expended on the Central Experimental Farm, but it carries on work of great benefit to the whole country. I think that in that Central Farm we have one of the best establishments that can be found anywhere. Only last summer, a prominent and well known agriculturist of Great Britain visited Ottawa, and, with a letter of introduction from me to the Director of Farms, he went to the Experimental Farm and looked over our livestock and the work that was being done. On his return he stated that, so far as he was aware, there was no establishment of this kind anywhere in the world, and certainly not in Great Britain. The farmers here, he said, had a tremendous advantage in having experimental work carried on for them, in having new lines produced, new cereals, new fruits, new vegetables and roots, such as he saw out on the farm, and so forth. All this information, after it is gathered together, the farmers have absolutely free of charge, and we have in Canada a tremendous opportunity for the development of agriculture. There are very many new areas in certain provinces where land and climatic conditions vary to a great extent. A settler may come from England or, say, the state of Alabama, and if he landed in those parts of the country and had no information, it would take him four or five years at least of valuable time getting established and studying the conditions prevaling there. All this time would be lost before he finally could get to work. With our experimental farm system he is able, at the outset, to obtain all the information necessary to take up the line of agriculture most suited to that particular section of the country. In
addition to that, he can obtain information as to the best varieties of seed to sow, how and when to sow it, etc. He can find out the best varieties of livestock to keep and the best method of marketing his products. I consider this a very great advantage.	Only last summer we had
a horticulturist from Oregon who came to Okanagan Valley in British Columbia and visited the station at Sum-merland. After examining the methods carried on there in connection with dry farming and irrigation, he stated that he was well acquainted with all the various farms in the United States, and that in future he would come to Summerland for his information because the work carried on there was better and more reliable than that of any other farm he knew of on the continent of America. Now, take this particular farm which the hon. member for South Oxford referred to. I may say that we have no fewer than thirteen branches there of various lines of work, from experiments in connection with horse breeding down to the breeding of bees and the production of honey. To give one example of the splendid work done on our farms; I may say that the average Canadian hen is responsible for only 65 eggs a year. Out on the farm at Sidney in British Columbia last year, the hens produced, by careful breeding and selection, no fewer than 300 eggs a piece. If we had failed to take advantage of the opportunities that presented themselves in this matter we should never have got anywhere, and our agriculture in this, as in other lines, would drag along in a listless sort of way. You may take a horse to the water, but you cannot make him drink, and if the farmers of this country have not life enough to take advantage of the opportunities that offer, and to secure all the information they can from our farms, then it is their own fault. I am sure there is no intelligent farmer who can go to the Central Farm, look over the livestock and see the methods of agriculture that are practised there without gaining considerable important information, whether . he farms on Vancouver Island or on Prince Edward Island.

How many experimental
farms are there in Canada?

There are twenty-one
regular farms, two tobacco stations, seventy-five illustration stations, and six or seven sub-stations.
What kind of hens-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

I might mention the
methods practised in connection with grain and vegetable plots. These plots are only about one-fortieth of an acre in extent, so small that you cannot use machinery to advantage on them. A new variety of grain may be secured from some other place and an experiment is made to find out whether it would be useful in this country. In addition to that particular plot there would be a number of other check plots planted at the same time, and this goes on from year to year. It is obvious, therefore, that a great deal of work is involved in keeping the place in proper condition, and information is not released until such time as the director of the farm is absolutely certain that what he has to impart is perfectly reliable and that anyone may make use of the information he gives, no matter whether he is in British Columbia or in Nova Scotia. This makes necessary considerable very fine work; it entails a great deal of hand labour, and naturally it means a lot of expense. After the experiments have been carried out the results are applied under field conditions, and the information obtained in consequence is published so that anyone may secure it for the asking, either through the mails, or directly from the farm. I feel sure that these farms are rendering a very valuable service, and a great many men derive considerable benefit from them. Of course, one cannot expect any profits from experimental work of this kind, requiring such minute care and attention, although many of the sections, such as our livestock and dairying sections, and the hog, sheep, and poultry sections, frequently yield a profit.

I do not want the minister to misunderstand me. I am not condemning the experimental farm system. I have always upheld that system, and have been a strong advocate of its extension, but when I refer to the Central Farm in Ottawa I have in mind the fact that you can go westward in Ontario and not find another Dominion experimental farm except a small tobacco farm in Western Ontario for the growing of tobacco. Even the operations of that are confined to a part of two counties and consequently its influence does not extend very far. Just a word or two with regard to those people in western Ontario who are so dense that they cannot follow the example that has been set them here in Ottawa
[Mr. Tolmie.l
and elsewhere by the experimental farm system because they, have not had the advantage of visiting the farm, unless they happened to come to this city, although there is a big stretch of the province of Ontario between its western limits and the city of Ottawa that separates the two and consequently conditions are not very similar. I might, for example, refer to the factory output of dairy products in a certain little spot of western Ontario-the county of Oxford-and to the fact that it equaled for the year 1917, which is the last that I have, the factory output of the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, British Columbia, and almost that of Prince Edward Island. So that as far as the farmers of that part of Canada are concerned, they have evidently been keeping pretty well abreast of the times bearing in mind the result of their labours. What I have objected to is that the experimental farm system is not brought home to the people, and that they do not have an opportunity of reaping the advantage they should derive from the money that has been expended here. I do not say that Ontario has been neglected. As I pointed out, and have repeatedly pointed out, we are doing the things that the Dominion ought to do for us, seeing they are doing those very things for the rest of the provinces. That is the exception I take to this enormous expenditure of over a quarter million of dollars on the farm at Ottawa which plays but a very small part in farming operations so far as the province of Ontario is concerned.

I cannot altogether agree
with my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) in his criticism that there has been extravagant expenditure on the farm adjacent to this city. I think the time has passed when it is necessary for any member of this House to defend the expenditures of the Federal Government on agriculture. If I had any criticism to offer, it would be that in my humble opinion the Government have not yet risen to the height which the country should demand of them-and that applies not only to the present Administration, but to Governments that have preceded them. There has always been an insistance upon the curtailment of expenditures when it came to agriculture:	I was glad to hear
the minister's remarks and his defence of the experimental farm. In his speech he touched on the question of poultry, and

having some knowledge of that industry, as well as some interest in it, I recently made a little study of its development in this country. I was influenced to do so more particularly by reason of the fact that last week I was booked to address a gathering of four or five hundred poultry men in the city of London. In connection [DOT]with the inquiries I made I was informed that the production of eggs in this country last year amounted to 2,244,000,000. Dividing this number into dozens we have 187,000,00 dozens of eggs; and then dividing that number.into cases of 30 dozen each it yields a total of 6,233,333 cases, or 15,555 carloads. But, Sir, I find that statistics show that the production of poultry in this country for the year 1920 amounted in value to the enormous sum of $120,000,000. The development of the poultry industry in Canada, and its expansion during the past few years, has been largely due to the splendid work of the experimental farm, and here I give credit to my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) for the legislation that was introduced a year or two ago, whereby the standardization of eggs was brought about, as being a matter of immense value to the poultry industry. I was speaking to the official in charge of the farm here upon the egg production in Canada, and the effect that the standardization of eggs had on our foreign markets. He told me that in the British market the Canadian egg standardized commanded a price of from eight pence to one shilling a dozen more than American eggs from the South. I asked him how the production of eggs in the United States and in the warmer climates compared with production in the colder climate of Canada. He replied that our production was not only better but that the quality of the egg was very much superior. The earliest census of poultry taken in this country goes away back to the year 1695 when in old Acadia there was a total of only 362, but in 1891 we had 12,696,701 in this country. According to the census returns in 1901 the number had increased to 16,651,337; in 1911 it was 29,773,457; and in 1920 the estimated figures of the poultry of the country were 45,000,000 head.
Now we find that this country last year imported a large number of eggs, the total importation amounting to 6,515,928 dozen, having a value of $3,051,833. It wouid seem to be a most regrettable thing that a country of such enormous resources as ours should have to import eggs for its own consumption. But it must be borne
is mind that in 1920 we exported 6,324,838 dozen, having a value of $4,198,430. Our import of eggs showed an average cost of 46.8 cents per dozen, while the export of eggs from this country, by reason of the standardization of our eggs and by reason of their superior quality, obtained for our exporters an average price of 66.3 cents. So that we export our eggs on the basis of 66.3 cents and import them on the vasis of 46.8 cents.
The work done on this experimental farm in Ottawa is not measured by what is produced there, we all know that, and I just simply illustrate the poultry division as only one item amongst many in which the advice given by the management of the experimental farm has been of enormous potential value to this country-a value that it is almost impossible to conceive. I say, success to the experimental farm at Ottawa! I agree with my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) that it is desirable to establish demonstration farms in practically every township if possible, but that work comes largely under the purview of the Provincial Governments, and their work, assisted by the Federal Department of Agriculture, has resulted in very great benefits to our farmers. I trust that this department will not in any way relax their efforts. My hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar), I notice, is somewhat critical of the expenditure and would economize by reducing the staff; but our expenditure here is nothing at all in proportion to the expenditure on agriculture in the United States, and if we are to develop this great country to its fullest possibilities in agriculture it is obvious that there should be no curtailment so long as the money is wisely used in the development of our experimental farm system.
I cannot agree with the previous speaker when he says that model farms in various sections of the country-
I said demonstration farms.

that demonstration farms should be left entirely to the Provincial Governments. I sympathize with what the hon. member for South Oxford has urged, that we should spend less on these experimental farms and more on demonstration farms all over the country. Why? The minister has just given the reason. On these experimental farms experiments of a very expensive character are conducted, so expensive that the ordinary farmer could not undertake them on his own farm. If

I read correctly the Auditor General's Report, we spent last year $375,000 on the Central Experimental Farm at Ottawa. In my opinion this item could have been reduced by over $100,000, and still, experiments on the scale I have described could have been carried on to whatever degree necessary for the purpose of enlightening our farmers. If instead of spending that $375,000 on the Central Experimental Farm the Government had devoted $100,000 or $200,000 in demonstrating in various sections of the country better methods of agriculture and in encouraging farmers by instruction and premium to grow better crops and raise better stock to suit local conditions, greater benefit would have resulted to the country generally; and even had the expenditure been greater than the amount in question it would have been thoroughly justified, because no matter how well the experimental farm in Ottawa is conducted only a very small number of our farmers can afford to visit it and derive personal benefit from the experiments there being carried on. The minister has told us that a distinguished gentleman from England visited the farm last year and expressed regret that they did not have such a farm even in England. Well,
I think this country should be satisfied with what they have in England so far as demonstration farms are concerned. We should not indulge in such luxuries as are exhibited at the Central Experimental Farm. We could easily dispense with a number of these items of expenditure and use the money all over the country for the great advantage of the many rather than as at the present, for the benefit of a few.
In the riding which I have the honour to represent we have an annual exhibition in the month of September which is assisted by the Provincial Government. The provincial department of agriculture send their specialists who give to the farmers very valuable information-information which can be utilized by our farmers to suit local conditions. Prizes are given for the best crops and also for school gardens, and every year the farmers can see the results of the best farming in every parish. But no matter what experiments are carried on at the Central Experimental Farm in Ottawa, very few farmers can afford to visit the farm even once in ten years. That is one reason why I sympathize very much indeed with the idea put forward by my hon. friend from South Oxford, that we should reduce the expenditure on our experimental farms and apply 
the money saved to increasing our demonstration farms so that their benefits may be brought home to every locality.
The Federal Department of Agriculture must have at heart the development of agriculture in all sections of the country, and that development is not being promoted to the fullest extent by conducting experiments here in Ottawa where climatic conditions are very much at variance with those prevailing in many other sections of the country. I would urge that the Government reduce their extraordinary expenditure on the experimental farms and devote the money to establishing more demonstration farms.

It is very evident that the speaker who has just taken his seat does not know anything about farming. He speaks as though the experimental farm at Ottawa was just for the benefit of a few local people.
Mr. Chairman, I want to correct the hon. gentleman. I never said any such thing.

The experimental farm at Ottawa has sent samples of grain and shrubs and seeds all over the Dominion. When the hon. gentleman speaks about school fairs in his riding, I may tell him that we have them in my county, and most of the children who plant their seeds in the school plots get those seeds from Ottawa. While I am opposed to extravagant expenditure in any line, I make the statement that when hon. gentlemen get up and talk respecting farming, it is evident that they never did any farming in their lives, or they would not complain about this expenditure of $350,000.

I wish to correct the hon.
gentleman. My father was a farmer; I was brought up on a farm; my ancestors were farmers for three hundred years.

It seems strange that most professional men in this House and out of the House claim that they were raised on the farm. I can certainly vouch for the fact that most of them were milked on the farm, anyway. I think hon. gentlemen are making a great mistake when they find fault with an expenditure of $300,000 or $350,000 on an industry which supplies as much as two-thirds of the wealth of this country. When the Government propose to spend three or four times as much on agriculture as was spent by past governments, we should commend, not criticize them. When I came to this House

ten or eleven years ago, less than one million dollars was spent on agriculture; now I believe we spend between five and six. It the money is wisely spent, no hon. member should find fault with a policy of that kind.
But there is one thing I do deplore-the fact that, as the minister says, the Civil Service Commission select the men for the different branches of this department and arrange their renumeration. I am sorry that the minister is not in a position to select better men to fill positions in his department than those who never farmed a day in their lives. Why are two or three men selected to sit in Ottawa and carry on the business of branches of which they know nothing whatever? We have a glaring example of that kind of thing in hon. gentlemen who get up in this committee and talk about the hours and the time and the holidays. Of course, a lawyer comes into his office at about ten o'clock in the morning, goes out at four or five and counts it a day, but the farmer has to work all day. These speeches that are being made about hours and time and holidays are doing more to hurt the farmers of Canada than anything else that could be done, because they are causing dissatisfaction among our men on the farms who are hired by the month or by the year. There are times when the people in the towns and cities would go hungry if the hired men on the farm did not work fourteen hours a day. I do" not know whether these fifteen days' holidays are supposed to be the legal holidays or whether they are over and above the holidays, but when a man is hired by the month or by the year on the experimental farms he is suposed to work a month or a year and he is supposed to get the legal holidays and no more. Something has been said about a man not being able to get away if a friend had died. Well, I know that in the county which I represent, if a hired man on the farm lost a relative by death the farmer would leave the work in the field and let him go, and our government would do the same. This talk about six or eight hours a day is driving our boys and girls off the farms; making them believe there is pleasure and nothing to do in the cities, and slavery and misery on the farm. I resent that kind of thing. I have spent most of my life on the farm and I say that there is no place where a man can have a better time or enjoy life better than on the farm. I hope that hon. gentlemen who get up to talk about farming and about agricultural
matters generally will be men who know something about farming. ,

My. hon. friend intimates
that I do not know the first thing about farming.

Oh, no, he was referring
to the member for South Oxford.

Both of us, I think, can give him some pointers on farming. The lecture of the hon. gentleman was quite unnecessary. I did not criticize the expenditure of $375,000 for the farming industry, though my hon. friend sought to create the impression that I did. I would like this Government to cut out some foolish expenditure that is proposed in other departments and use the money for the development and improvement of the agricultural industry in this country. I am not criticizing expenditure in respect to experimental farms, but I would like these experiments to be carried out not merely at one central point, but in demonstration farms all over the country, because that would result in greater benefit to the farming community at large. Coming back to my hon. friend's suggestion that I do not know the first thing about farming, I do not like to blow my own horn as the hon. gentleman has blown his, but I may tell him that my ancestors came to this country in 1657 and were all farmers. My father was a farmer; I was brought up on a farm. I own a farm of my own, and am proud of it.
What about your grandfather?

I have said that all my
ancestors were farmers; that should be sufficient for my hon. friend. I think it most improper, therefore, that an hon. gentleman should jump and say that we do not know the first thing about farming. Why, the hon. gentleman himself was ignorant of what he was talking about. He was throwing stones into the garden of his neighbour though he was himself inhabiting a glass house. Let him learn the lesson; let him go a little more slowly when he is impelled to make such remarks with regard to hon. gentlemen on this side.

Mr. Chairman, if the committee is to understand that the minister accepts the statement of the hon. member for West Quebec that these messengers gather eggs, in approved committee style I shall have to add another question and ask how many eggs they collect. But that is

just in line with what I really wanted to ask. I notice in going over the list that there are about 125 stenographers in the department and about 11)0 clerks. Even the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best) will admit that I know a little about this subject, even though I might not know so much about farming. I would like to ask the minister whether in his department there is any return of the number of letters or pages of typewriting which are turned out by this staff of 125 stenographers? Is any return made to the Civil Service Commission of the number of entries which these clerks are obliged to make? When the chief of staff in a large financial institution is asked whether a certain branch may have an additional junior officer, he can immediately go over the work of that office and determine whether or not the answer should be in the affirmative-and this without making any personal visit to the office. I think some such arrangement should prevail in the Civil Service I have made the suggestion before and I make it again now upon the coming before this committee of the first department's work. I should like and I am sure the committee would like to know whether any return of this sort is made or asked for from the departments, and I trust the minister will not forget my question about the messengers.

We can furnish this information, but we cannot do it offhand. If the hon. gentleman wants it, I shall be glad to give it to him. As regards the duties of messengers, they are used in the usual way, in carrying messages from one office to another in the different departments which are scattered over the city. They are used in connection with the mail and so forth, along all the general lines for which a messenger is used. The messengers in our department are all steadily engaged and, so far as I know, they are rendering good service. In answer to the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), as I have explained before, while we carry on these small experiments on the big experimental farm, they are afterwards tried out under field conditions and the information obtained is given out to the country. The hon. member speaks of what is being done now by the provinces in the way of demonstrating agriculture to the farmers. They use what are known as county representatives who travel about from one farm to another. We assist the provinces at the rate of one million dollars a year for improving agricultural education, some of this money being

used in the way I have mentioned. As regards the work carried on at the experimental farms, not only can a man go there and look at the plots in which these experiments are being conducted, but he can also see the work that is being done under field conditions. For instance, the production this last year of an average of thirty' tons to the acre, of sunflower at a cost of less than $3 per ton placed in the silo, is a demonstration that any practical farmer can benefit by. In addition to that, the crop of oats ran about eighty or ninety bushels to the acre grown under certain conditions. Clover was also grown under different conditions and calculations made as to the cost of production. Therefore, the experimental farm, in addition to demonstration work, is of great use to the practical farmer who wishes to visit it. The money expended at the Central Experimental Farm covers a wide scope in addition to what is done on the farm. For instance, it covers the tobacco farms at Farnham and Harrow. It covers the work at the illustration stations, of which there are seventy-five scattered throughout Canada. It covers the flax extension work, the potato inspection work, the rot investigation work, and it also covers a very important work we carry on for the education of the farmers. It covers the exhibits which are taken from our experimental farms to all the principal fairs in Canada, and we have with those exhibits demonstrators who describe the methods under which the plants are grown or the way in which wool is cared for after it is taken from the sheep and carded. We also demonstrate the candling of eggs and so forth. Any hon. member who has attended any of our large fairs in recent years will probably remember some excellent exhibits from those forms, and that is taking the demonstration to the doors of the farmers. On those seventy-five illustration forms scattered throughout Canada very excellent work is done, showing the farmer exactly how to use the best methods under actual farming conditions, and the experimental farms and illustration stations are cooperating very well together. In addition to that, we cooperate with the governments of the various provinces in many lines of work, and we oftan afford them great assistance which they use to good advantage.

I wish to say a word or two in connection with this expenditure of $375,000. I may differ from some hon.

members on both sides of the House in regard to this matter. My opinion is that the Central Experimental Farm should be the best, not only in the Dominion of Canada, but in any part of the world; When we are expending a few hundred thousand dollars on the Central Experimental Farm in the city of Ottawa, we are only carrying out a policy that has been laid down by the great ministers of agriculture that we have had, not only in the Liberal party, but in the great Conservative party, ever since Canada has been a nation-
Hear, hear.

-Or a young nation. As regards the argument that we should cut down this expenditure, I say to hon. gentlemen who are objecting to it, that we might as well be conducting the affairs of Canada in the Museum a few blocks away as conducting the affairs of Canada in this magnificent Parliament building which we have caused to be erected at a cost to the people of Canada of millions of dollars. When we stand up in this Parliament to-night and object to paltry expenditures of this kind, we are simply playing into the hands of the big interests of the country who are standing back and laughing; we are giving them a certain amount of amusement to think that we, as supporters of agriculture in Canada, are differing in regard to backing up the Minister of Agriculture as long as he carries on the affairs of his department honestly and well. When the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Best), whose views and ideas I have supported on many occasions, speaks about patronage, I say that the agricultural department should be conducted in the way in which it is being conducted, namely, by the Civil Service Commission; that patronage should be cut out, and that men who are qualified and who are deserving of promotion should be given the preference, instead of some partisans whose position or advancement may be advocated by hon. members opposite or by members on this side after members on this side come into power. I am in sympathy with giving the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Tolmie) every assistance possible, belt) p.m. cause I am convinced that when he is fighting his Estimates through Council, he has his troubles, and while other ministers may smile, I believe they will agree with me that what I say is absolutely right. There is a great work for the Minister of Agriculture to do in this country, not merely for the general encouragement of greater production, but for bringing that production to such a point that there will be a reduction in the cost of living to the people of Canada, and without giving such assistance, we shall be unable to achieve that result. As regards extravagance in connection with our experimental farm, I am in favour of giving the minister every possible assistance, even if he does spend a few dollars more than we might see fit to endorse at this particular time. Experimental plots are absolutely necessary. This Parliament, not the Government, has already voted $1,000,000 to be distributed amongst the various provinces in order that they may carry on experimental farms so as to encourage the growing of crops that are particularly adapted for different sections throughout Canada. We have given that money; we are voting it to-night without discussion, and then we are hesitating to say that we stand behind the minister in carrying out the work he is going to do for the great purpose of agriculture which we all profess to be behind to the last. I am in sympathy with this expenditure, even if it may seem extravagant, because I believe the minister is doing the best he can under the circumstances.

As a representative of a rural constituency 1 chink I ought to say something on this subject. I agree with almost every word that ha,s been said by my hon. friend from Kent (Mr. Mc-Coig). I would ask the minister to consider a proposition which has been put before him on many occasions by myself and others on behalf of the people of the County of Charlevoix-Montmorcney, and that is to reopen the demonstration farm which was established there some time ago, in 1913, or 1914, if I remember correctly, but which was discontinued. I have never yet been able to find out why it was discontinued, hut since I have been a member of this House I have tried on many occasions to get the farm opened, without success.
Mr. Chairman-
I should like an answer from the minister.

I must point out that questions concerning the establishment or re-establishment of demonstration farms have already been ruled out of order on this item. If any question concerning the expenditure of the Department of

Agriculture may be asked on item No. 14, the entire discussion can be started over and over again every time the Estimates of the Department of Agriculture are before the committee. Item No. 14 which we are now considering deals solely with Civil Government expenditure here in th>

On page 89 of the Estimates there are two items: "Veterinary Director General, $5,040" and "Chief Veterinary Inspector, $3,900." I understand that these are two separate positions occupied by two different men. I should like to know when the office of Chief Veterinary Inspector was established, where the official lives, and what his duties are?

The name of that officer is Dr. George Hilton. He resides in Ottawa and has occupied the position for about 12 or 14 years, roughly speaking. This particular office was created before I became minister; I cannot say how long it has been in existence. The duties of the office are to assist the Veterinary Director' General, and to act in his absence when he is out of town. Dr. Hilton assists in a great deal of the outside work at the various quarantine ports, and in connection with the field inspection work that is carried on throughout Canada.
The minister has told us that there are 70 odd illustration stations in Canada. How many are in Ontario, and how many in Quebec?

The Department of Agriculture has no illustration stations in the province of Ontario. The Commission of Conservation has been carrying on some work along that line, and so long as thev were doing that the department did not interfere. The proposed changes will perhaps result in a new policy in that direction. We have 30 illustration stations in the province of Quebec at the present time.

Before this item passes I should like to satisfy my curiosity with respect to one statement made by the minister in his very eloquent and inter-
[The Chairman.]
esting remarks a few moments ago. He stated that years ago hens in this country were producing 65 eggs per year, and that now in some cases they are producing 300 per year. That is very important, I think, and I should like the minister to tell the committee, so that the country at large will know, what special strain it is that produces this large number of eggs per year.

The particular breed

for me to ask the minister what this gentleman does?
His name is Dr. Malte. He is an expert of very great ability in that line?

I was just coming to the line. His business is the study of grasses and different varieties of plants, and there are some very interesting examples of his splendid work on the farm. He crosses various kinds of grasses, plants, etc., the general business being the production of fodder plants. He has done most excellent work in improving timothy and clover.

An hon. member on
the other side said to-night that the frequency of our questions to the minister might be interpreted as an opposition to the agricultural estimates. I do not consider that I have to give any explanation of my attitude, because what I have done to-day is only what I do every day; I have performed what I consider to be my public duty by my constituents and by the people of the country at large. But should our attitude on this side, and the attitude of the committee, have had only the result of giving to the minister an opportunity to explain, as fully and as lucidly as he has done, every item in regard to which he has been questioned, I think that we have reason to be very well satisfied. My hon. friend from Kent (Mr. McCoig) has said that hon. members on both sides would gladly support the minister in the administration of his department, and with that statement I fully agree. Agriculture in this country, as the member for Kent has said, is not only important, but essential. We all understand that. I represent a farming constituency, and although I have not the honour to be a member of the farming community of Canada, I have great sympathy with the farmers. I understand their needs and try to help them to the best of my ability. Let us hope that so long as we have a government in Canada we shall always have as competent a minister as the hon. gentleman who now holds that office. The ministers at the head of the Department of Agriculture in past years were most remarkable men in many ways. We had the Hon. Sidney Fisher, who has left a name for himself. That hon. gentleman administered his department in such a way that he has shown the road that has been followed ever since by his successors. I have nothing to say in the way of compliment to the former 60
Minister of Agriculture, who is now leader of the Agrarian party (Mr. Crerar). On his departure from the department, my hon. friend from British Columbia was called to the Cabinet. To-night we have asked the minister many questions and he has very frankly and good-naturedly answered them, and I say that he has shown our country that the present Minister of Agriculture is just as efficient and competent as any minister we have had before.

That farm was closed up before I assumed my present position. I regret that I cannot give my hon. friend an answer off-hand, but I will try to get information on the subject.
Would it be possible to have a station established in that district? What are the prospects?

In the very near

I do not wish to burden my hon. friend with faults that may have

He had some pull.

Mr. Chairman, I do not expect the minister who is a serious business man, to establish twenty-five farms in my constituency, or one farm in each parish; but I should be most grateful to this Government if it would redeem the promise made to my constituents a few years ago by one of its former members. I know that some farmers in my county would like to take advantage of the system if it is still being continued by the department.

That is an item that comes properly under livestock. Under our sys-

tem pure bred sires are distributed in dis tricts where no such sires are available, usually in outlying new districts. Our system is for the farmers to form a club of ten members and on their showing that they have a proper number of cattle and that their farms are suitable for rearing stock, we loan them a bull and pay the freight on it to their nearest station. One of the farmers maintains the animal during the three or four years it is left in the district, and then it is moved to some ither section. That has been found to work to the very great advantage of our farmers, particularly those in outlying new districts. I have in mind such districts as that on the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. A large number of settlers have gone into that country, and under ordinary conditions it would have been a matter of ten years before they would have enough money to purchase a pure bred sire-and they would at the end of that time still have scrub stock on their farms. But under this system of the distribution of pure bred sires we are furnishing sires to such districts as these in the first year of their settlement, so that in five or six years the cattle up there will be high grade cattle, not scrub stock, and the livestock wealth of Canada' will be materially increased.
